claim: BSurfaces (guide-stroke-based retopology): draw annotation strokes crossing perpendicular guide strokes across a region needing new topology, click 'Add Surface', then adjust the Cross/Follow segment counts and enable 'Cyclic Cross' to bridge the first and last stroke into a closed loop -- this generates a full ring of quads conforming to the surface in one operation instead of building it polygon by polygon. Organic-topology-specific in this source (eye socket on a sculpt), but the same guide-stroke approach applies to any closed opening needing controlled edge-loop density.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched full video): at 1:15-1:33, guide strokes drawn around an eye opening plus 'Add Surface' with Cyclic Cross enabled produces a closed ring of quads conforming to the contour in one operation.
rejected_alternative: Building the closed ring of quads polygon by polygon

claim: In BSurfaces, drawing one guide stroke in the opposite direction from its neighbors (start-to-end order matters, not just position) produces a twisted, self-intersecting X-shaped quad in the generated strip. Fix: select the flipped edge in Edit Mode and press S (scale) then scale it through/past its own origin (a negative-scale flip) to reverse its vertex order, rather than deleting and redrawing the stroke.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 3:45-4:08, one stroke drawn in the opposite direction from its neighbors produced a twisted X-shaped face; scaling the flipped edge through its origin reversed its vertex order and fixed the strip without redrawing.
rejected_alternative: Deleting and redrawing the mis-directed stroke from scratch
reason: The twist is caused specifically by inconsistent start-to-end stroke direction, not by wrong vertex positions -- reversing the existing edge's order fixes the actual cause directly instead of starting over.

claim: The F2 add-on: with a single active corner vertex selected on the boundary of an existing quad strip, pressing F predicts and creates a new quad face snapped to the underlying surface directly from that one vertex (rather than requiring multi-vertex selection), and moving the mouse before confirming positions the new corner -- pressing F repeatedly zips out an entire new row of connected quads extending from a boundary loop.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 5:27-5:53, selecting a single boundary corner vertex and pressing F repeatedly extends an entire new row of quads along a boundary loop, each snapped to the sculpt surface.
rejected_alternative: Extruding edges through the normal multi-step select-and-snap process
reason: F2's single-vertex quad prediction is significantly faster than manually selecting and snapping each new quad's worth of geometry when expanding topology outward from an existing boundary.

claim: LoopTools' Circle (forces a selected loop into a radial/circular distribution), Relax (smooths jittery step-like spacing), and Space (equalizes distance between vertices along the loop) can be applied in sequence to clean up an irregularly-spaced edge loop -- all three preserve the loop's attachment to an underlying Shrinkwrap-projected surface rather than detaching it.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 6:08-6:29, an irregular edge loop around an opening is cleaned up by applying LoopTools Circle, then Relax, then Space in sequence, all while staying shrinkwrapped to the surface.
rejected_alternative: Manually repositioning each vertex along the loop to even out spacing

claim: Viewport vertex snapping only recalculates during an active transform (G/R/S) -- newly-created geometry from a non-transform operation (e.g. a Ctrl+R loop cut) sits on the flat chord between existing points and is NOT automatically snapped to a curved reference surface. A live Shrinkwrap modifier (Project mode) in the object's own modifier stack, by contrast, continuously re-projects ALL vertices including brand-new ones onto the target surface in real time, with no separate snap step needed.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 8:05-8:25, a Ctrl+R loop cut with only viewport snapping active leaves new vertices on a flat chord, but with a Project-mode Shrinkwrap modifier active on the same object, the newly-inserted loop-cut vertices immediately snap outward onto the curved high-poly surface without any extra step.
rejected_alternative: Relying on viewport vertex snapping alone to keep new geometry on a curved reference surface
reason: Viewport snapping is a per-transform behavior and doesn't cover geometry created by non-transform operations like loop cuts; a live Shrinkwrap modifier covers every vertex continuously regardless of how it was created.

claim: During a Shrinkwrap-projected retopology workflow, a mesh's true (un-projected) base-mesh vertex coordinates can drift far from the reference surface over time as edits accumulate, causing projection glitches (vertices ray-casting to the wrong spot) especially in tight crevices or overlapping forms. Maintenance fix: periodically duplicate the Shrinkwrap modifier and apply the top copy (baking the currently-projected positions into the actual base mesh data) while leaving a second live Shrinkwrap modifier below it (and below Mirror, if present) for continued work.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 8:31-8:58, the Shrinkwrap modifier is duplicated and the top copy applied (baking projected positions into the base mesh) while a second live Shrinkwrap remains below the Mirror modifier, preventing base-mesh vertices from drifting far off the sculpt surface over continued editing.
rejected_alternative: Continuing to edit indefinitely on top of a single live Shrinkwrap without ever baking the projected positions in
reason: Letting the true base-mesh coordinates drift arbitrarily far from the reference surface (while only the projected/evaluated result looks correct) eventually causes ray-cast projection failures in tight or overlapping geometry; periodically baking the projected result back into the base mesh keeps the underlying data close to the surface.

claim: Sculpt Mode's 'Slide Relax' brush, applied directly to a retopologized mesh (not the underlying sculpt), tangentially redistributes bunched-up/uneven quad density across the surface without changing the mesh's outer volume or detaching it from the reference surface -- a faster alternative to manually repositioning individual vertices in Edit Mode to even out topology density.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 12:12-12:56, the Slide Relax brush in Sculpt Mode is used directly on the retopo mesh to redistribute uneven, bunched-up quads across a surface region while preserving the outer volume and surface contact.
rejected_alternative: Manually repositioning individual vertices in Edit Mode to even out quad density
reason: Manual per-vertex repositioning is tedious and risks distorting the surface; the Slide Relax brush relaxes the whole local topology network tangentially across the surface at once.
